## Introduction

Is there a linear relationship between a college's graduation rate and its faculty's average salary? 

## Preprocessing

The College dataset is large and mostly clean, but several steps need to be prepared before beginning analysis. Since my research question focuses on whether a college’s graduation rate is related to the average faculty salary, the first step is to single out only the columns needed for this analysis. I selected the variables C150_4 (graduation rate) and AVGFACSAL (average faculty salary) and saved them into a dataset for easier analysis.

Because the original dataset uses its own column abbreviations, I renamed the variables for organization purposes. This makes visualization and modeling steps easier to understand. Neither of my variables are categorical, so I didn’t need to do any recoding for this project. I also did not remove rows with missing values because the instructions say to wait until later in the analysis before filtering out NAs


```{r}
# Select the columns I need for my analysis
college_reduced <- college %>%
  select(C150_4, AVGFACSAL)

# Rename them to the variable names I want to use
college_clean <- college_reduced %>%
  rename(
    GRAD_RATE = C150_4,
    AVGFACSAL = AVGFACSAL
  )


college_clean <- college_clean %>%
  mutate(
    GRAD_RATE = GRAD_RATE * 100
  )

```


## Visualization

```{r}

ggplot(college_clean, aes(x = GRAD_RATE)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "pink", color = "black") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Graduation Rates",
    x = "Graduation Rate Percentage",
    y = "Count of Colleges"
  )

```
The histogram shows that graduation rates vary widely among colleges. Most institutions fall between about 30% and 70%, with fewer colleges having extremely high or extremely low rates. The shape is slightly right-skewed, meaning more colleges have mid-range graduation rates than high ones. This variation suggests that many factors influence graduation rates, which makes it important to check how faculty salary relates to this outcome.



```{r}
ggplot(college_clean, aes(x = AVGFACSAL)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1000, fill = "purple", color = "black") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Average Faculty Salaries",
    x = "Average Faculty Salary (US Dollars)",
    y = "Count of Colleges"
  )

```

The histogram shows that most colleges pay between $40,000 and $80,000 on average. There are fewer colleges with very high salaries, which makes the distribution slightly right-skewed. This suggests that salary levels vary noticeably between institutions, and these differences could affect factors like student success and graduation outcomes.


```{r}
ggplot(college_clean, aes(x = AVGFACSAL, y = GRAD_RATE)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, color = "red") +
  labs(
    title = "Graduation Rate vs. Average Faculty Salary",
    x = "Average Faculty Salary (US Dollars)",
    y = "Graduation Rate Percentage"
  )

```

The scatter plot shows a positive trend. Colleges that pay higher average faculty salaries tend to have higher graduation rates, although the points are somewhat spread out. This shows that faculty salary might play a part in student success, but it is unlikely to be the only factor. The moderate spread of points suggests other variables may also influence graduation rates.


```{r}
ggplot(college_clean, aes(x = AVGFACSAL, y = GRAD_RATE)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, color = "darkorange") +
  facet_wrap(~ LOCALE) +
  labs(
    title = "Graduation Rate vs Salary by Region",
    x = "Average Faculty Salary (USD)",
    y = "Graduation Rate (%)"
  )

```
